transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: ok hi everybody thanks for joining, happy Tuesday. quick roll call?
[00:08] Rita Alvarez: Rita here, samir and jonas are on from infra.
[00:11] Samir Patel: hey, Samir -- sorry bit of ring delay.
[00:16] Jonas Meyer: Jonas, CTO, hi.
[00:18] Liam Ortega: Liam from Redwood SE, hi all.
[00:22] Maya: Cool. Agenda — quick review of last weeks tuning, the retune we pushed for continuous batching, then go over the burst test results and next steps.
[00:32] Rita: That sounds good. We really want to see how it behaves under a sudden shopping-cart style surge, like 40 qps to 600 qps over a couple minutes.
[00:39] Maya: Yep. Liam, can you kick off with the telemetry highlights?
[00:42] Liam: Sure. Let me pull up notes — so the run from last thursday, we did three steady windows and one synthetic burst. Steady windows: mean tokens/sec per GPU about 1.8k, p95 gen latency 220 ms for short prompts (under 64 tokens). During the synthetic burst we saw queue depth climb to ~180 requests on the host, batch sizes increased up to 48, but tail latencies degraded to p95 ~1.6s and p99 spiked near 4.8s.
[01:15] Samir: just to check, when you say batch size 48 is that across the worker pool or per GPU?
[01:20] Liam: across the batching pool on that slot; basically continuous batching pooled requests before slice-to-gpu. We did observe some skew — a few GPUs had larger micro-batches because of routing.
[01:30] Jonas: was KV cache hit rate good during the burst? that often kills us if it's low.
[01:34] Liam: Hit rate fell from 68% steady to 36% in the first 60s of the burst, so more cold starts. That coupled with larger seq lengths for some requests amplified tail. Also we suspect our prefix caching knob wasn't aggressive enough, so KV cache warming lagged.
[01:50] Rita: that's rough. so the cold starts are the bigger issue vs batching?
[01:54] Liam: it's a combo. Continuous batching helped throughput — overall tokens/sec went up — but because requests accumulated the queueing delay + cold KV misses pushed effective end-to-end latency up. So we have to balance concurrency target to allow batching benefit without creating excessive queue queuing.
[02:12] Maya: Okay, quick primer for the stake holders — continuous batching trades small latency for better GPU utilization; if queue builds you get increased client-side wait. We can tune the batching wait threshold and max batch size, and also adjust concurrency target (how many inflight requests per GPU) to avoid over-commit.
[02:28] Samir: what numbers are you suggesting as conservative vs aggressive?
[02:31] Liam: conservative: concurrency 8 per GPU, max batch 24, batching-wait 8ms. aggressive: concurrency 24 per GPU, max batch 64, batching-wait 18ms. Our last test was in the middle: concurrency 16, max batch 48, wait 12ms.
[02:48] Jonas: the p99 was unacceptable for our external facing api, we need sub-2s target at p99 for short queries.
[02:54] Maya: noted. that's our SLO target for this pilot.
[02:58] Rita: also cost. higher concurrency and large batches may reduce tokens cost but increase cold starts when models switch, and we have compliance concerns on Private vs Hosted.
[03:07] Maya: right. We also did a quick baseline comparing Hosted vs Dedicated under the same config: Dedicated removes noisy neighbor routing volatility and gave 8-12% more stable batch sizes — but Dedicated pricing has the usual commit. We'll send pricing scenarios.
[03:23] Samir: on the security lane: we need to confirm KMS handling for embeddings and model input logs, plus SSO and audit trail. jungle of compliance.
[03:32] Maya: we have SOC2 + SAML docs, we'll share the security pack after the call.
[03:35] Liam: back to telemetry: GPU util during the burst averaged 78% with spikes to 96% — so GPU was fairly busy, but the idle gaps came from KV misses and reloading. We tracked model swap events — a couple of small swap windows when the runtime rotated local cache.
[03:52] Samir: model swap? like swapping weights in memory?
[03:54] Liam: yeah internal memory management when the runtime evicts cold segments; we saw a 200-400 ms penalty per affected request. Could be tuned by pre-warming the KV cache for top prefixes.
[04:05] Rita: what's our plan to improve KV cache hit rate?
[04:07] Liam: Options: 1) increase hot-key prewarm policy (warmer threads push top-k prefixes into KV on schedule), 2) reduce eviction aggressiveness, 3) tweak routing to keep affinity — stick related requests to same GPU to leverage warm KV. Prewarm + affinity gave the biggest wins in our internal tests.
[04:24] Jonas: affinity makes sense, but does that risk imbalance across GPUs?
[04:26] Liam: yes can cause imbalance; we can combine soft-affinity with burst-aware rebalancing — when imbalance exceeds threshold we rebalance.
[04:33] Maya: we captured histograms for request inter-arrival times — synapse traffic has a heavy tail with microbursts every 7-12 minutes from batch jobs. That pattern explains cold windows.
[04:43] Samir: we'll upload a 48h sample trace for you to analyze.
[04:46] Rita: next, latency buckets. can you remind us of how we can set concurrency per API route?
[04:51] Liam: yes per-route concurrency is supported; we can pin low-latency routes (e.g., interactive chat) to conservative concurrency and give higher throughput routes more aggressive settings. That was part of the pilot config we recommended.
[05:03] Jonas: would routing by route require extra infra or is it config on Redwood side?
[05:07] Liam: it's config — you can set policies in the Redwood Console to route by path header or token. Under Dedicated it runs locally so no additional infra changes for you.
[05:15] Rita: ok good.
[05:16] Maya: Quick detour — we noticed an error pattern during the burst where some requests returned truncated responses or early EOS; could be timeout in the batching window. Liam any idea?
[05:25] Liam: yes we saw short-window timeouts; the runtime default hard timeout was 6s in that job; with the p99 spiking, some requests hit the client-side timeout. We recommend increasing server-side request_timeout to 12s for the burst windows and setting client-side to 10s to avoid mid-response truncation.
[05:39] Samir: fine but that increases tail exposure.
[05:41] Maya: tradeoff. We'll only do that for the controlled burst.
[05:45] Rita: Speaking of controlled burst — what's your test plan?
[05:47] Liam: propose: 30 minute run with a 10 minute warmup ramp, then a 5 minute sustained x32 concurrency peak, then 15 minute cool down. We'll collect per-GPU batch distributions, KV hit rates, GPU mem pressure, p50/p95/p99, and the queue depth traces.
[06:03] Jonas: do you need access to our VPC?
[06:05] Maya: for Hosted no; for Dedicated if we spin up in your VPC we'll need peering or private link — we can run the burst in Hosted first then replicate in Dedicated if you want.
[06:16] Rita: let's do Hosted first and then run the same config on Dedicated. We want to see the delta.
[06:20] Liam: noted. I'll schedule tests for tomorrow morning UTC if that's ok.
[06:24] Samir: tomorrow morning works. We'll also share traffic trace by EOD today.
[06:28] Maya: Great. Any blockers on security?
[06:31] Jonas: need confirmation about log retention and PII stripping; our legal team needs to see the audit logs format.
[06:36] Maya: we'll attach the audit-log schema with the security pack.
[06:39] Rita: one more thing — cost. can you give a rough delta for concurrency 8 vs 24?
[06:44] Liam: rough ballpark: with continuous batching tuned, concurrency 8 would be about 1.0x baseline cost per token, concurrency 24 could drop unit cost by ~20-25% due to higher batch efficiency but with higher tail latency and more memory pressure possibly causing evictions — so you'd pay less per token but risk SLO violations unless affinity and prewarm are in place.
[07:06] Jonas: Alright. Syntax question: can Redwood export the raw batch traces as CSV?
[07:10] Liam: yes, we'll provide CSV with columns: timestamp, route, gpu_id, batch_size, queue_depth, kv_hit, p50, p95, p99.
[07:18] Samir: perfect.
[07:20] Maya: anything else on tuning knobs?
[07:22] Liam: small things — tweak max_sequence padding policy to reduce wasted compute for short prompts; dynamic quantization profile we tested shows small perf wins but not dramatic.
[07:34] Rita: when do you think we can hit our p99 < 2s target?
[07:37] Liam: if burst test goes as planned and we enable prewarm + affinity, we should see p99 drop from 4.8s to ~1.6-1.9s in hosted within 48 hours of tuning. Dedicated should be faster once we run the same config.
[07:50] Jonas: good.
[07:51] Maya: ok recap — Sean? (laugh) Samir said he'll upload traffic trace by EOD today; Liam to run burst test x32 tomorrow morning and share CSV + GPU logs; Maya to share pricing and security pack; Synapse will review the logs and decide whether to progress to Dedicated pilot. We'll book follow up next thursday.
[08:12] Samir: noted. do you want a weekly cadence after that?
[08:15] Rita: yes weekly until steady-state.
[08:18] Maya: Great. I'll send calendar invites — wrap up any final questions?
[08:22] Jonas: none from me.
[08:23] Rita: good meeting. thanks.
[08:25] Liam: thanks all.
[08:27] Maya: bye.
